opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think Carl and I agree on a lot of the basic structure here, and then disagree somewhat on the speed and on how much of it is driven by software versus hardware.

The core picture, which I find pretty compelling, is this: once you have AI systems that can do the work of AI researchers, you get a feedback loop. Better AI makes AI research faster, which makes better AI. And there's a lot of room for software improvement. Historically, algorithmic progress has been comparable to hardware progress in reducing the compute needed for a given level of performance. If you suddenly have millions of copies of very capable researchers working on that, it seems plausible you could compress what would have been years of algorithmic progress into months.

Where I'm more uncertain is the returns. The key question is roughly: when you double the research effort going into software, how much do you improve the software, and does that improvement more than pay for itself in terms of effective research capacity? If returns are good enough, you get something like a hyperbolic takeoff purely in software, without needing to build new fabs. Carl's estimates suggest they plausibly are. I think that's a live possibility, maybe even the most likely single scenario, but I put real weight on returns diminishing faster than that. Ideas get harder to find, you hit limits on how efficient a given amount of compute can be, and experiments themselves need compute, so you can't just throw more researcher-copies at the problem indefinitely.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that I expect the run-up to be more continuous than people sometimes imagine. Before you get AI that fully automates AI research, you get AI that's automating 30%, 50%, 80% of it. So things are already speeding up noticeably before the explosion proper. That doesn't necessarily make the end phase slower, but it means the world probably looks pretty crazy, with big economic impact and a lot of investment, before the really fast part. I think that matters a lot for how we should prepare.

So overall: I take the fast software-driven scenario seriously, maybe I'd say there's a substantial chance we go from roughly human-level AI researchers to something radically superhuman within a year or so. But I'd put meaningful probability on it taking longer and being more bottlenecked by compute and hardware scale-up, which plays out over years rather than months. And from a safety perspective, the fact that it could be that fast is a strong reason to want our alignment and oversight work in good shape well before we get there, because you might not get much time to course-correct once the loop is running.

r001.rationale: The response says it disagrees with Carl on speed and software versus hardware, but never clearly says it assigns a lower probability than Carl to the very fast scenario. It calls that scenario a substantial chance and perhaps the most likely single scenario.

r002.rationale: The response describes a gradual ramp in AI automation before full automation, but does not identify a longer period of complementarity between AI and human capabilities as a factor that would soften takeoff. It even says the ramp does not necessarily make the end phase slower.

r003.rationale: The response names diminishing software returns and says takeoff could be more bottlenecked by compute and hardware scale-up. It does not identify scaling electricity production as part of the takeoff.

fable-5.1.text:
I think Carl's picture is, in its broad strokes, pretty plausible, and I'd say I'm closer to agreeing with him than most people in the field are. The basic argument is that once AI systems can do the work of AI researchers, you've closed a feedback loop: the output of the research is better researchers, and so you get a very rapid acceleration that doesn't need to wait on building new fabs or new power plants. Just the software side, running on the hardware you already have, can take you a very long way. And I think that's right as a matter of the structure of the situation. The question is about the parameters.

Where I'd put more probability than Carl is on things being slower and messier than the clean story suggests. A few reasons. One is that the returns to software progress are uncertain. We have some evidence from the historical record about how fast algorithmic efficiency has improved, something like a doubling of effective compute every year or so from algorithms alone, and the question is how much of that is low-hanging fruit that gets picked before you have armies of automated researchers. If the easy gains are already taken, then even a huge increase in research effort buys you less than you'd naively extrapolate. Carl would say, I think, that the historical rate was achieved with a fairly small number of people and there's a lot of room, and that's a reasonable position. But I hold more uncertainty about how diminishing the returns get.

A second thing is that I'm not sure the transition is as sharp as "now the AIs can do the research." I expect a period, maybe a couple of years, where AI is doing a large and growing fraction of the work but humans are still in the loop in important ways, where the systems are good at some parts of research and bad at others, and where the bottlenecks shift to things like running experiments, which still need compute. Compute for experiments is a real constraint. If your automated researchers have great ideas but each one needs a big training run to test, you don't get to run a thousand times more experiments just because you have a thousand times more researchers. So I think the actual speedup during the transition is more like a factor of a few to maybe ten rather than the hundreds or thousands you'd get in the fully software-limited regime.

The third thing I'd say is that even conditional on the dynamics being roughly as Carl describes, I think there's a lot of practical friction. Labs make decisions, governments get involved, things get slowed down or redirected for reasons that have nothing to do with the technical feasibility. That cuts both ways, since it can also mean a race, but it adds variance to the picture.

So my overall view is something like: I think it's quite likely, more likely than not, that the period from "AI is doing a substantial fraction of AI research" to "AI is radically superhuman" is short by historical standards, a few years rather than decades. But I'd put a lot less weight than Carl on the very fast end, where it's months, and more weight on the version where it's several years of really intense, confusing, and quite dangerous progress. And honestly that's the scenario I find most worth preparing for, because it's fast enough that our institutions will struggle but slow enough that the decisions people make during the transition actually matter a lot.

r001.rationale: The response says it puts less weight than Carl on the very fast, months-long scenario and more on a takeoff lasting several years.

r002.rationale: It expects a couple of years when AI does a growing share of research while humans remain important, with bottlenecks limiting the speedup.

r003.rationale: It discusses uncertainty and diminishing returns in software progress, but does not say those returns could make scaling electricity or hardware production part of the takeoff.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic picture is pretty plausible. Once AI systems can do most of the work involved in improving AI, you have a feedback loop: better systems let you do research faster, which produces still better systems. And software improvements are especially interesting because you can deploy them without waiting to build another generation of data centers.

The question is how much improvement you get each time around that loop. You could have AI researchers doing ten times as much work, but if the experiments they need still take months, or if the next improvements are much harder to find, that doesn’t immediately translate into another tenfold increase in capability. There’s a difference between making the cognitive work cheap and making the whole research process fast.

So I’m sympathetic to Carl’s picture, but I’m less confident about the very fastest versions. I’d want to know how much room there is for software improvement on a fixed amount of hardware, how effectively you can substitute reasoning for experiments, and how quickly the returns to additional research diminish.

I also think you can get an extraordinarily consequential transition without the strongest version of the intelligence explosion. Going from AI that’s somewhat helpful for research to AI that does almost all of it over a few years would already be a very big deal. Whether that subsequently compresses into months or weeks is important, but I wouldn’t want uncertainty about that last step to obscure how fast the less extreme scenarios are.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the picture is plausible but expresses less confidence in its fastest versions; it does not clearly say its probability is lower than Carl Shulman’s.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses experiments taking months and the limits of speeding up the whole research process, but does not identify a longer period of complementarity between AI and human capabilities.

r003.rationale: The candidate mentions diminishing returns and software improvements on fixed hardware, but does not connect diminishing software progress to scaling electricity or hardware production as part of takeoff.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic picture is plausible. Once you have AI systems that can do most of the work involved in improving AI, you could have a much faster feedback loop than we have today. You’re no longer waiting for more humans to become researchers, and you can potentially run a lot of copies of your best researchers.

The part I’m more uncertain about is how fast that translates into better systems. There’s a difference between having a million researchers and making a million times as much progress. They need experiments, those experiments take compute and time, and a lot of research depends on the results of earlier research. So the key question is how much progress you can make by thinking harder with the hardware you already have, versus how much requires larger training runs or more hardware.

Carl’s picture seems most compelling if there’s a lot of room for software improvements, and if better AI researchers can find those improvements quickly. Then you could get a substantial acceleration before building any new chips. I take that possibility seriously. I’m less confident about a particular timeline—whether that process takes weeks, months, or years. Those differences matter a lot, and I don’t think the feedback-loop argument by itself settles them.

r001.rationale: The response calls Carl’s picture plausible and expresses uncertainty about the timeline, but does not assign it a lower probability than Carl does.

r002.rationale: It says AI could reduce the need to wait for more human researchers; it does not identify a longer period of AI–human complementarity as softening takeoff.

r003.rationale: It mentions compute, time, larger training runs, and hardware, but does not identify diminishing returns to software progress or scaling electricity and hardware production as part of takeoff.
